# E046 -- US Army Corps of Engineers Visual Identity Standards

## Metadata
- **Company:** US Army Corps of Engineers
- **Industry:** Government / Military
- **Year:** 1994
- **Source file:** us-army-corps-of-engineers-pdf.pdf
- **Pages:** 82
- **Language:** EN
- **Pages sampled:** 1-2, 6-7, 12-13

## Brand Strategy
- Titled "Graphic Standards Manual" -- EP 310-1-6, revised September 1994, with Change 1 dated June 2006
- Official Department of the Army pamphlet (CECW-CO)
- Purpose: uniform graphic identification system for internal Corps audiences and the general public
- Communication Mark registered with US Patent and Trademark Office (Registration No. 1,807,986, November 30, 1993)
- Centralized control: Graphic Standards Coordinator at HQUSACE, CEIM-IV provides advice on all applications
- National Sign Program Manager at St. Paul District (per 2006 change)

## Logo
- **Communication Mark** -- key graphic element, derived from traditional castle symbol used since Corps inception
- Redesigned as "simplified contemporary rendering of a traditional symbol" for strength and adaptability
- Three preferred configurations:
  - **One-Color Version:** mark + signature in a single dark-value color; black or dark primary/secondary colors preferred; avoid pastels
  - **Two-Color Version:** mark in Communication Red, name in black on white; for two-color or four-color process printing
  - **Reverse Version:** special drawing with additional white outline to prevent castle rendering as black in negative
- Minimum size: never less than 1/4" in height
- Must be reproduced by photographic processes from approved art (Chapter 9); grid drawing provided for oversized applications
- Never rotated from proper axis
- No prior versions of Corps mark may be used
- No Division, District, or Field Operating Activity symbols/marks may be used
- The (R) symbol required on printed promotional material for public usage
- Assets available in diskette format

## Typography
- Not covered in sampled pages (likely in later chapters)

## Color
- **Communication Red** -- primary accent color; achieved in four-color process as solid magenta / 80% yellow
- Swatches for matching provided in Chapter 9
- Dark values of primary or secondary colors preferred for one-color applications
- Tone and Color Usage Guide on page 1-5

## Graphics
- **Heraldic Symbology** -- Chapter 2 covers historical and traditional Corps symbols
- Multiple graphic symbols available beyond the Communication Mark:
  - Historic symbols and coats of arms appropriate for presentations requiring sense of tradition
  - Communication Mark conveys contemporary, modern government agency image
- Decision framework: choose symbol based on "desired effect of your presentation"
- All symbols available in diskette format

## Photography
- Not covered in sampled pages

## Applications
- Publication covers (mark may stand alone, but full signature must appear elsewhere -- back cover, spine, or title page)
- Identification, promotion, and advertising applications
- Signs (National Sign Program with dedicated managers)
- Full signature used as primary identification for Field Operating Activities

## Tone of Voice
- Formal, bureaucratic, military-standard language
- Directive: "shall", "may be used", "should never be"
- Hierarchical: all decisions flow through Graphic Standards Coordinator

## Outliers
- **1994 document** -- one of the oldest brand guidelines in the collection, with 2006 amendment
- "Diskette format" for asset distribution -- period-appropriate digital asset management
- Registered trademark on a government agency mark -- unusual for public sector
- Heraldic symbology chapter provides decision framework for choosing between modern and traditional symbols
- Reverse version requires specially redrawn mark (not just a simple color inversion) -- technical sophistication for pre-digital era
- Communication Red achieved as solid magenta / 80% yellow -- precise CMYK recipe rather than a PMS reference in sampled pages
- 82 pages for a government manual -- exceptionally thorough

## Quality Score
- **3/5** -- Comprehensive government graphic standards manual with meticulous technical specifications for mark reproduction; strong historical context; loses points for dated format, no digital/web guidance (understandably, given 1994 origin), and limited coverage of typography, photography, and modern applications
